title: Family photographs and heirlooms; Moscow landmarks
description: Agnes Hailey Jones shows Isabel Miller photographs of the log cabin where she was born, her grandfather's ice cream parlor in Moscow (now a Safeway parking lot), her 50th birthday cake, and family members including her mother and grandson. They confirm Jones's mother was the first white child born in Latah County. Jones says she sold the old homestead land.

title: Personal background; parents' history; father's accident
description: Jones gives her full name, birth date of January 16, 1890, and Genesee address, and explains her husband Harding, 95, is now in a rest home. She describes being born in a rustic log cabin northwest of Genesee while her father lay in the corner with a fractured leg from falling off a haystack; his leg was later amputated in Spokane. She gives biographical details for her mother Annie Tierney, born 1871 at Thorn Creek and the first white girl born between Moscow and Lewiston, and her Irish-born father from County Kerry.

title: Mother's farm labor; parents' livelihoods
description: Jones recounts the heavy work of her young mother, who weighed about 105 pounds, carried water to 25 hogs, milked cows, made and sold butter, and maintained the farm while the men cut winter wood and split rail fences near Troy. Her father delivered milk in Genesee and raised hogs and cattle. She names her three sisters and recalls Genesee when it was new.

title: Husband's background; marriage; children
description: Jones describes her husband Harding B. Jones, born in Philadelphia in 1880, who worked as a streetcar construction foreman in Spokane before they married there in 1910. She names her three daughters, Eva, Thelma, and Mary Agnes, born in Spokane and Colfax, and outlines their careers and husbands' work, including a dairy near Colton and teaching in Seattle.

title: Education; store and restaurant work in Spokane
description: Jones explains she left school after about eighth grade and, before marriage, worked in Spokane grocery stores and cooked hotcakes and waffles while cashiering on Sprague Avenue for over two years. She says she liked the work and enjoyed meeting the public.

title: Poultry raising; feather curing; produce and egg sales
description: Jones details raising over 800 geese on the ranch, dressing them, curing feathers for pillows and mattresses, and shipping geese, ducks, and turkeys to Spokane buyers. She also sold butter to regular customers, milked and broke in cows, raised fryers and flowers in Spokane, made sauerkraut, and crocheted cushion covers for sale, saying she always had something to bring in money.

title: Health; sewing for family; clubs and awards
description: After noting her surgeries and high blood pressure, Jones says she had no hobbies because the days were never long enough; she sewed all her daughters' clothes and remade donated dresses. She lists her memberships in the Eastern Star, Latah County Pioneers Association, and Moscow museum, her presidencies, fair booths, and parade appearances playing an old reed organ.

title: Small-town life; farm versus city; animal care
description: Jones reflects on Genesee's changes as old friends die and newcomers arrive, and compares farm life, which she likes for its independence and animals but finds lonely, with her twelve years in Spokane. She recounts doctoring geese stung by bees, reviving chilled pigs under the stove, and stresses understanding the nature of animals.

title: Current daily life; childhood memories of money
description: Jones describes her present routine, with daughters calling daily and trips to the rest home and doctor, and recalls how scarce money was in her childhood, when her mother traded butter and eggs for groceries. She notes all her sisters graduated from school and are now scattered.

title: Courtship and marriage; childbirth; daughters' families
description: Jones recalls meeting her husband at the cashier's desk in Spokane, courting, and marrying at nearly twenty after her health broke down, and says married life turned out all right. She had her babies in hospital maternity wards, nearly dying in Colfax, and contrasts this with her grandmother who died in childbirth in 1874; she praises her daughters, sons-in-law, and grandchildren's accomplishments.

title: Views on modern young people; grandchildren's work
description: Jones thinks parents today give children too little companionship, and praises her grandson with an MD in agronomy and the Colton dairy family's milking machines, which she learned to use from her granddaughter. She describes granddaughters' jobs at WSU and in catering, noting they keep busy like she always did.

title: Recreation; family life; farm finances and the move from Spokane
description: Jones describes television, newspapers, family pets, and children staying close to home, then explains how her father offered the couple 240 acres to bring them back from Spokane to farm. She recalls buying lumber and planning the house, farming her own 120 acres, and refusing her husband's wish to sell out and move to California after a hailstorm destroyed their crop.

title: Community involvement; advice for farm women; furniture refinishing
description: Jones touches briefly on her organizational involvement and fair ribbons, then advises that farming is a business in itself, too hard for women not raised to it, and that a farm wife must be half the partnership. She describes stripping varnish and rebuilding secondhand furniture in recent years, her favorite television programs, and making decisions jointly with her husband before the interview closes.

title: Poultry raising; predators and pests
description: Agnes Hailey Jones describes setting an incubator for duck eggs and the arrival of wild mallards. She recounts how skunks and coyotes attacked her chickens and geese, killing them by biting their necks, and explains the necessity of burying dead animals to avoid attracting bears.

title: Hunting skunks; coyote behavior
description: Jones explains that she did not trap skunks but shot them with a shotgun when they threatened the chicken house, recalling specific nighttime encounters. She notes that her grandchildren now trap skunks for their valuable hides, and describes how coyotes would snatch poultry but generally avoid humans.

title: Grandfather's homesteading; prairie chickens
description: Jones recounts her grandfather's homesteading days, when prairie chickens were so abundant they could be caught under a wagon box. She describes how Native Americans would prepare these birds by coating them in mud and cooking them on bonfires.

title: Portrait sketch; antique roller organ
description: The interviewer shows Jones a sketch drawn of her, which Jones views with amusement. Jones then demonstrates a 78-year-old roller organ inherited from her grandfather, playing "Turkey in the Straw" and explaining that she has refused to sell the instrument despite offers from collectors.
